# On the Peculiar Art of Being Human

There's a moment that happens to everyone, probably multiple times throughout their life, where you become acutely aware that you exist. Not in a philosophical sense necessarily, though it can be. I mean the sudden, jarring recognition that you are a conscious being inhabiting a physical body, moving through space and time, making decisions that ripple outward in ways you'll never fully understand. It happened to me recently while standing in a grocery store, looking at rows of pasta sauce.

I was thinking about nothing in particular—which sauce to buy, probably, or whether I'd forgotten something on my list—when I noticed an elderly woman two aisles over reaching for something on the top shelf. She couldn't quite reach it, and a young man nearby helped her without being asked. Just a small kindness. And suddenly I was struck by the improbability of it all: the woman, the man, me, all here simultaneously, all conscious, all navigating existence according to our own mysterious internal logic, all going to die someday. The grocery store suddenly felt like a beautiful, strange museum of temporary consciousness.

This is the thing about being human that I find most remarkable and least talked about: we're all just making it up as we go along.

We have this tendency to mythologize certain people as if they were made of different stuff than the rest of us. We imagine that artists and scientists and leaders and innovators somehow possess a clarity or certainty that eluded the rest of humanity. But I think the truth is more interesting. I think everyone—even the people whose names are remembered, whose work shapes history—is fundamentally confused most of the time. They're guessing. They're following hunches. They're doing their best with incomplete information and faulty memories and contradictory emotions.

I read once that David Bowie had tremendous anxiety throughout his life, even at the height of his fame and success. Here was a man who created some of the most innovative music of the twentieth century, who reinvented himself repeatedly, who seemed to exist on a different plane than ordinary people. And yet he was anxious. He doubted himself. He struggled. This somehow made him more impressive to me, not less.

The alternative—that some people are just naturally, transcendently confident and certain—seems not just false but spiritually impoverished. Because what would be the point of growth, of learning, of art, of conversation, of any of the things that make life worth living, if some people started from a position of complete understanding? The entire human project is predicated on incompleteness. We create because we don't understand. We reach out to others because we're lonely. We build relationships because we're vulnerable.

I think we've gotten this backwards. We've convinced ourselves that the goal is to achieve some state of arrival, some final answer, some permanent certainty. We imagine adulthood as a destination rather than an ongoing process. But adulthood is just more childhood, really, only with higher stakes and better knowledge of how things actually work. And even that better knowledge is partial, contested, subject to revision.

The people I admire most aren't the ones who claim to have answers. They're the ones who are genuinely curious about the right questions. They're the ones who can sit with uncertainty without needing to rush toward false comfort. They're the ones who change their minds when presented with new information, not as a sign of weakness, but as evidence that they're actually thinking.

One of the strange things about human consciousness is that we're the only animals we know of who are fully aware that we're going to die. Every other creature presumably has some sense of danger, some instinct for self-preservation. But only we know that no amount of caution will ultimately save us. We're mortal, and we're aware of it, and somehow we have to build meaningful lives in the face of that fact.

This could be depressing, and sometimes it is. But I've found that it's also oddly liberating. It means that the things we're anxious about—the meeting we're dreading, the social interaction we're afraid might go badly, the job we're worried we're not doing perfectly—don't actually matter that much in the grand scheme. Not in a nihilistic way, where nothing matters. But in the sense that we're all just trying to do our best, and that effort itself is the point.

I watch people do remarkable things all the time, often without realizing how remarkable they are. A parent staying up all night with a sick child. A friend listening to you talk through the same problem for the hundredth time without sighing. Someone holding the door for a stranger. These gestures don't require special talent or education or privilege. They just require showing up, being present, extending your attention to another person.

There's this Protestant work ethic that permeates our culture, this sense that the goal is to be productive, to achieve, to accumulate. And don't get me wrong, there's nothing wrong with work, with creation, with building something. But we've turned it into a kind of religion. We've decided that our worth is measured by our output, our productivity, our climbing some ladder that never actually reaches anywhere. We're convinced that if we're not constantly improving ourselves, constantly optimizing, constantly grinding, then we're falling behind.

But behind what? And toward what end?

I think a lot of human misery comes from chasing metrics that don't actually measure anything important. We'll never be thin enough, rich enough, successful enough, because "enough" is a place that doesn't exist. We're running on a treadmill that someone else built, trying to reach a finish line that keeps moving away from us.

Some of the happiest people I've known are people who have somehow opted out of this game. Not completely—they still need to earn money and maintain relationships and navigate the basic structures of society. But they've stopped treating life as a problem to be solved. They've decided that the point is the living itself, the actual experience of being alive, not some hypothetical future state where all their concerns are finally resolved.

This is maybe the hardest thing to learn, because we're taught from a very young age that the point of childhood is to prepare for adulthood, and the point of being an adult is to achieve certain markers of success, and then... well, then you've made it, I guess. You get to finally live. Except by then you're exhausted, and retirement is distant, and there's always another thing that needs to be accomplished first.

What if we just stopped? What if we decided that right now, today, in this imperfect moment with all its limitations and annoyances and failures, we're exactly where we need to be?

This isn't an argument for passivity or complacency. But I do think there's a difference between ambition that comes from a place of joy and ambition that comes from a place of fear. One drives you toward something. The other drives you away from something. And the one driven by fear is never satisfied, because fear is never satisfied.

I've been thinking a lot lately about the stories we tell ourselves about who we are. We seem to have this idea that personality is fixed, that we're certain ways and we'll always be that way. I'm shy. I'm bad at math. I'm not creative. I'm not the kind of person who can do X. And then we spend our lives acting in accordance with these stories, treating them as if they're objective truths rather than narratives we constructed, often based on limited evidence or a single bad experience.

But people change. People are constantly changing. You're not the same person you were five years ago, or even last year. You have different thoughts, different priorities, different relationships. And yet we treat ourselves as fixed objects, as if we're made of something unchangeable.

This is both terrifying and exciting. It means you're not locked into being whoever you've decided you are. But it also means you have to take responsibility for who you're becoming, moment by moment. You can't blame it on your personality or your upbringing or your circumstances, not entirely. You're always, at some level, choosing.

What strikes me most about human existence is how much of it is just about connection. We're social creatures, and I don't mean that in the way that's sometimes meant pejoratively (like, you're only social because you're insecure). I mean that consciousness itself seems to be fundamentally about connection. We understand ourselves through our relationships with others. We're lonely without community. We make meaning together.

The most profound moments I've experienced have almost all involved another person really seeing me, really hearing me, or me doing the same for them. Not fixing something or solving a problem or achieving some external goal. Just the simple fact of being understood, of being known.

There's a quote from the writer David Foster Wallace that I think about sometimes: "The so-called 'psychotically depressed' person who tries to kill herself doesn't do so out of quote 'hopelessness' or any abstract conviction that life's assets and debits do not square. And surely not because death seems suddenly appealing. The person in whom It awakens experiences a certain indescribable psychic pain, a pain that is often unendurable. It is impossible to achieve the same level of closeness with other people that we have with our own minds."

The thing he's pointing to—that gap between inner and outer experience, between what's happening inside and what we can communicate to others—is both the source of much human suffering and the reason we keep trying to connect anyway. We know we can't fully bridge that gap, but we keep reaching across it because the alternative—complete isolation—is unbearable.

I wonder sometimes if that's what art is for. Not as decoration or entertainment or status, but as an attempt to build a bridge, to make visible what's invisible, to say "I feel this too" across the void of individual consciousness.

When I listen to a song that moves me, or read something that captures something I've felt but never been able to articulate, I feel less alone. Someone else has been here. Someone else has felt this. They've taken the time to shape it into something that could reach me across whatever distance separates us. That's an extraordinary gift.

Being human is strange and difficult and more often boring than we'd like to admit. We spend a lot of our lives waiting for things—waiting for the future, waiting to become the people we're supposed to be, waiting for life to finally start. But life is already happening. It's happening right now, in this moment, while you're reading these words. And it's already almost over, statistically speaking. The average person will live for maybe 27,000 days. We'll spend about a third of them sleeping. A lot of the rest will be taken up with basic maintenance—eating, cleaning, working, moving from place to place.

The remainder—the remainder that's actually available for living, for experiencing, for creating meaning—is smaller than we think.

This is why I've become less interested in certainty and more interested in presence. This is why I've started saying yes to more things, even things that make me nervous. This is why I've become more curious about people who are different from me, more interested in really listening instead of just waiting for my turn to talk.

Because I think the point of being human isn't to solve the problem of being human. The point is to live through it. To taste food and notice light and connect with other people and make things and ask questions and be confused and try anyway. To accept that we don't get a final answer, that the mystery doesn't resolve, that we'll die not knowing most of what we want to know.

And somehow, that's okay. Somehow, that's actually beautiful.

We're all just here together, making it up as we go along, trying to be kind to each other while we figure it out. That's enough.
